title: Dos grados
label: ch:es-abrigo
canDo: I can act on a cold-weather reading: take a temperature in degrees off a bus-stop screen, and choose between a jacket, a coat and a scarf on the strength of the number rather than a general impression.

payoff.summary: Read a bus-stop screen and a message from home, then decide what to put on.
payoff.note: THE WARDROBE WAS DECLARED COMPLETE AT CHAPTER 430 AND THIS CHAPTER REOPENS IT ON PURPOSE. ES-C430-repaso-piezas is headed 'the wardrobe, complete' and ends 'The list an exam works from is now covered end to end' -- pantalon, falda, camisa, zapato, vaqueros, jersey, bolso. That was true FOR A1, which asks you to DESCRIBE what you are wearing. A2 asks you to DECIDE, and deciding needs a number, so this chapter adds the outerwear weather requires plus the unit that triggers it. The repaso says this out loud rather than extending a closed list in silence. (Note the 430 list was never an inventory of taught garments either: el vestido, la camiseta, el gorro and la ropa are all taught and absent from it, and el gorro is the pointed omission since it is winter headwear belonging to this chapter's own theme, so 'end to end' was always an exam-scope claim.) CHAQUETA HAS ALREADY BEEN USED IN PROSE TWICE and must be cited, not introduced: a table row in ES-C430-jersey and "Una chaqueta de piel is a leather jacket" in ES-C300-piel. CAREFUL WITH THAT TABLE -- ES-C430-jersey heads it 'clothing words that name a PLACE' and its third row is 'la chaqueta | a French peasant named Jacques'. Jacques is a PERSON. jaquette -> jaque is firm; jaque -> Jacques is NOT -- a rival account runs through Spanish jaco to an Arabic word for a mail jerkin, and the lesson names both and carries the hedge into the gloss, the table and the wrap-up rather than dropping it after one paragraph, but the column header is wrong for that row and this chapter must NOT repeat 'place'. The etymology is also hedged here as the best available story rather than a proof, because the medieval French trail is not clean. EL GRADO HAS NEVER APPEARED IN CORPUS PROSE. Every prior hit is an IDENTIFIER -- the id ES-C60-repaso-grado, activity ids, a prerequisites entry -- so the learner has never been shown the word, and the lesson must NOT say 'the word you already had'. It HAS appeared in the temperature sense in the A1 and A2 mock papers, which is the gap this closes. NOTE ALSO: ES-C60- is a LEGACY MODULE ID, NOT a chapter number -- ES-C60-repaso-grado is chapter 229 -- so never derive a 'chapter N' claim from an ES-CNN prefix. And it is the same word: gradus is a STEP, so a thermometer is a staircase and the poco/bastante/muy scale is steps up a quality. ES-C465-temperatura taught the quantity WITHOUT its unit; this supplies it, with estar a (estamos a tres grados). Ir de grado is a different word, from gratus. EL ABRIGO is named for what it DOES, not its shape: apricari, to BASK IN THE SUN, apricus a sunny sheltered spot -- so el abrigo is a shelter you wear, and al abrigo de is the one you stand in. English apricot is NOT a relative (Arabic and Portuguese, from praecoquum) and the lesson says so, because the resemblance invites exactly that error. LA BUFANDA CARRIES roots: [] because its origin is unsettled -- French bouffante is the usual guess, Italian buffa another. The lesson must NOT claim the empty root list is itself the signal: 526 of 1476 Spanish lessons carry roots: [] and 332 of those give a settled etymology in the prose anyway, including this chapter's own prerequisite ES-C300-piel. The ledger is opt-in metadata and a lower bound, as lessons.d already records. The rule about leaving an origin OPEN is owned by ES-C450-patio ('an empty list is not an oversight in this material; it is a claim'), with ES-C439-anden, ES-C439-tirar and ES-C402-gorro as the precedents -- el gorro being the nearest, winter headwear whose origin the Academy also marks uncertain. La bufanda is the fifth, and the lesson cites patio rather than staging the point as new. The payoff pairs a bus-stop screen (a number, no explanation) against a message from home (a decision plus a reason), and turns on 'ponte el abrigo, NO la chaqueta' -- Spanish correcting with nothing but no plus the thing ruled out. REGIONAL HAZARD, HANDLED: chaqueta carries a vulgar second sense in Mexico and much of Central America, so a variety: general lesson must give the neutral words (saco, campera, chamarra) in a table rather than teach it bare. For the same reason the model sentences use llevarse, not coger -- ES-C35-tomar warns that coger is coarse slang across much of Latin America, and these would otherwise have been the first sentences in the corpus to put it in the learner's mouth. The synthesis says estuviste ENFERMO, not malo: the corpus has taught malo as BAD only, and estar malo for ill is Peninsular colloquial. The causal que is NEW -- the learner's que is the relative one from ES-C53 and the taught reason-word is porque -- so la bufanda introduces it where it first appears, and the synthesis calls it the spoken stand-in for porque rather than 'the same que'.
